newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil vote on re-election bill seen delayed.
newsitem.headline: Brazil vote on re-election bill seen delayed.

text.p: The Brazilian government may have to delay until Jan. 29 this week's scheduled vote on a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for a second term, political analysts said.

Opposition to the timing of the re-election vote within the normally Cardoso-allied Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), the biggest in Congress, means the government cannot be sure of the three-fifths majority it needs in the lower house.
"My feeling is that it will have to wait until Jan. 29," said Marcelo Cordeiro, an analyst with Santafe Ideias.

Political observers were taken by surprise on Thursday when a senior whip said the government would put a constitutional amendment allowing re-election to a first of two votes on the floor of the lower house Jan. 22.

The move was seen as putting pressure on the PMDB which is split on whether its lawmakers can take part in voting on re-election until after upcoming elections for the presidencies of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.
"I don't think the government knows for sure exactly how many votes it can rely on," said Maria Teresa Sedek, a politics professor at Sao Paulo University.

Government whips were probably bluffing when they claimed to have more than the 308 votes needed for approval of re-election in the lower house because the position of the PMDB, which has 102 of a total 513 deputies, remained unclear, Sedek said.

The insistence by senior figures within the PMDB that the party only votes on re-election after the internal congressional elections has dashed the government's plan of getting re-election through both its lower house votes in January.

It now hopes to persuade the PMDB to vote once on the amendment in January, leaving the second vote until after the Chamber of Deputies and Senate elections which take place in the first week of February.

Cardoso called a special session of Congress to run through the January recess to deal with re-election in the Chamber of Deputies before the pro-reform president of the Chamber of Deputies, Deputy Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes steps down on Feb. 1.
The government also wants re-election approved quickly in order to resume progress on its social security, civil service and tax reforms which have been put on hold.
